title: Stock Trading With a Limited Number of Deals
statement:
`prices[i]` is the price of a stock on day `i`. You may complete **at most `k` transactions**, where one transaction is one buy followed later by one sell. You hold **at most one share** at a time (sell before buying again), and you may buy again on the day you sold.

Return the **largest total profit**.

examples.explanation: Buy at 1 and sell at 7 (profit 6), then buy at 2 and sell at 8 (profit 6): 12.
Prices only fall: no profitable transaction.

hints.nudge: How would you solve it for exactly one transaction? What do you need to remember about the number of transactions already used?
hints.pattern: Dynamic programming over (number of transactions, day): for each count t keep the best profit while holding a share (`buy[t]`) and the best profit after the t-th sale (`sell[t]`).
hints.walkthrough: Trying every choice of buy and sell days is exponential. Let buy[t] be the best profit so far if you are holding the share of your t-th transaction, and sell[t] the best profit so far after finishing t transactions. On each new price you can keep things as they are, or buy for the t-th time (starting from the best profit after t - 1 completed transactions, paying the price) or sell for the t-th time (cashing in the share held for the t-th transaction). Process the transactions for each day in increasing t; because you may buy again on the day you sell, using the updated buy[t] when computing sell[t] is allowed (it just means buying and selling on the same day, profit 0). The answer is sell[k]. This is O(n * k). If k is at least half the number of days it never binds, and you could simply add up every upward step; the table gives the same result.
